title: Office Fit-Up in Winnipeg: Planning Around Your Lease
metaTitle: Office Fit-Up Lease Planning in Winnipeg | Bridgeland
metaDescription: Plan a Winnipeg office fit-up around your lease: landlord consent, tenant allowances, City permits, inspections and the occupancy permit before move-in.
excerpt: How to line up an office fit-up with your lease dates in Winnipeg: what to settle with the landlord, which City approvals apply, and when your team can actually move in.
answer: Plan an office fit-up backwards from your lease. Before signing, get the landlord's consent to your plans, and settle what the landlord will build or pay for and who owns the improvements when you leave. Then allow time for drawings, a City building permit, inspections and an occupancy permit before your team moves in.

faqs.q: What is the difference between an office fit-up and a renovation?
faqs.a: A fit-up is the work that prepares a leased space for a particular tenant: walls, doors, lighting, power and data, finishes and sometimes washrooms or mechanical changes. A renovation can be any upgrade to an existing space. The approvals are the same either way: commercial interior alterations in Winnipeg go through a City building permit.

faqs.q: Who pays for an office fit-up?
faqs.a: It depends on the lease. Landlords may offer a tenant improvement allowance, often set per square foot, rent-free months, or turnkey work they complete before you move in. Whatever the landlord does not cover, you fund. Put the allowance amount, what it can be spent on and when it is paid into the lease itself.

faqs.q: Can we move furniture and computers in before the occupancy permit?
faqs.a: Furniture, yes; computers, no. The City's occupancy bulletin allows desks, workstations, chairs and tables to be delivered and installed before the permit, but not storing personal belongings, installing loose equipment such as computers, printers and copiers, training staff or meeting clients. Plan IT installation and your first workday for after the interim or final occupancy permit is issued.

faqs.q: Do I need an architect for an office fit-up?
faqs.a: Not always. Architectural drawings for a commercial alteration do not have to come from an architect unless the work is complex. The City's form lists the triggers, such as structural changes, significant fire alarm or sprinkler changes, or significant work on exits, corridors or fire separations in a Part 3 building. Then sealed drawings are required.

faqs.q: How early should we start planning?
faqs.a: As soon as you are seriously considering a space, and ideally before you sign. An on-site visit at that stage shows whether the layout works, what the building needs and which approvals apply. Bridgeland Builders offers that visit free, follows it with a free written quote, and replies to enquiries within one business day.

blocks.x: A fit-up, also called tenant or leasehold improvements, is the work that turns a leased space into your office: walls, doors, lighting, power and data, finishes and sometimes mechanical changes. The construction is only part of the timeline.

The lease decides who pays and what you may build, and the City decides when people can work there. Our [office renovation services](/services/office-renovations) page covers the build; this guide covers the planning around it.
What should you settle with the landlord before signing?

Get the landlord's consent to your plans, confirm the lease allows future changes, and find out what the landlord will contribute: a tenant improvement allowance, rent-free months or work done by the landlord. Also confirm which improvements stay with the building when you leave, because attached improvements usually do unless the lease says otherwise.

blocks.x: BDC also suggests confirming that the building can structurally support your work and equipment. On the City side, the permit application needs a letter of authorization from the building owner or property manager for your intended use, so landlord sign-off is part of the permit, not just the lease.
Does an office fit-up need a building permit in Winnipeg?

Usually, yes. Interior alterations in a commercial building go through a City building permit using the Commercial Alteration Design Summary (CADS) form, with electrical and mechanical permits taken out by licensed contractors. Significant work on exits, public corridors or fire separations in a Part 3 building, significant sprinkler or fire alarm changes and any structural change need sealed drawings.
Office projects have a few specifics. In a multi-tenant building, the form asks for your neighbouring tenants because fire separation requirements depend on their uses.

Tenant fit-ups in new Part 3 buildings need a Manitoba Energy Code for Buildings declaration. Projects exempt from a development permit file a declaration instead; otherwise the development permit can be reviewed before or alongside the building permit.

For simpler fit-ups, the architectural drawings do not have to come from an architect. The City asks for someone who can show the scope clearly and professionally: a key plan of where your unit sits, and a scaled floor plan with dimensions, labelled rooms and walls marked existing, new or demolished.

In September 2026, the City took an average of 5.3 business days to review minor alterations in Part 3 buildings (no change of use, no professionals required and no impact on life safety), against its own target of 5, and 6.9 business days for a change of use in existing tenant space, against a target of 15.

In a small commercial Part 9 building, three storeys or less with a building area under 600 m², the average that month was 6.2 business days against a target of 15. That's review time, not the total time until a permit is issued.
When can your team move in?

Only once the City issues an interim or final occupancy permit, where one is required. The City's occupancy bulletin lists installing loose equipment such as computers, printers and copiers, training staff and meeting clients as occupying a space. Our guide to [occupancy permits and change of use](/blog/occupancy-permit-change-of-use-winnipeg) explains when one is needed.

Construction and the delivery and installation of furniture such as desks, workstations and cubicle partitions are allowed earlier, but storing personal belongings is not, so plan IT set-up and move day around the permit.

Before you can request occupancy, the City's progress inspections must be complete to the final stage, and any architect or engineer involved must submit their professional certifications. The permit applicant requests the inspections, so build inspection dates into the schedule rather than treating the last week as finishing time.

blocks.x: Can an office be renovated while people keep working?

Often, if the work is phased and noisy tasks are scheduled carefully. Evening and weekend work keeps daytime disruption down, but within 150 metres of a home the City limits loud construction to 7 a.m. to 9 p.m. on weekdays and 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. on weekends and holidays. Building rules set by your landlord also apply.

Ask the property manager about elevator bookings, after-hours access and restricted tasks. If clients visit and an accessible entrance or washroom will be out of use, Manitoba's Accessible Customer Service Standard requires you to let the public know when and why.

Bridgeland Builders schedules commercial work in the evenings and on weekends where it helps and sends a progress update every week. More on staying open is in our guide to [preparing your business for a major renovation](/blog/how-to-prepare-your-business-for-a-major-renovation).
What should an office fit-up budget include?

More than construction. Include design and any engineering fees, permit fees, the build itself, furniture, IT and phone systems, moving costs, any rent you pay before you can occupy, and a contingency. BDC recommends setting aside a contingency fund and leaving buffer room in your timeline, because renovations often run over budget and past deadline.

If you need to borrow, our guide to [commercial renovation financing in Manitoba](/blog/how-to-finance-a-commercial-renovation-without-breaking-the-bank) compares term loans, leasehold improvement loans and landlord allowances. Office fit-ups are priced in a free written quote after an on-site visit, not from an online estimate; see what moves that price in [the biggest cost factors in commercial renovation projects](/blog/the-biggest-cost-factors-in-commercial-renovation-projects).
Questions to ask at the on-site visit
Can the layout reuse existing walls, doors, ceilings and lighting?
Will any work touch exits, corridors, fire separations or sprinklers?
Which tasks need after-hours scheduling under the building's rules?
What has to be finished before we can request occupancy, and when is that realistic?
